summary.text:
Gloucester City's 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy sits inside an Exceptional Financial Support application for £15.5m via capitalisation direction — the covering report says this is the only way the council can set a balanced budget for the year. The strategy carries a £345m authorised borrowing limit against a CFR forecast to peak at £285.993m in 2026/27, and continues an under-borrowing narrative.

The distinctive feature is the portfolio in Table 3.1: at 1 January 2026, of £228.2m of external borrowing, £109.5m (48%) is from other local authorities, £118.7m (52%) is PWLB and the £5m LOBO carried at 31 March 2025 has gone. Paper doesn't say whether the LOBO was called or discharged; either way it removes the twelve-month reset risk we've been tracking across councils we've read. PWLB balance is unchanged across the nine-month window — the movement has all been in the short-dated LA book and the LOBO.

Financing costs are budgeted at 37.17% of net revenue in 2026/27 and are attributed to the Kings Walk, St Oswalds and Forum retail investments. Maturity limits are set 0%–100% across every bucket — no active concentration constraint. On the standard CFR − external − OLTL identity the council is over-borrowed by £21m against a paper claim of £0.9m under-borrowed; the paper's calc omits OLTL from the deduction. Both financing-cost and identity observations are internal — neither belongs in a first contact with a council in EFS.

Reconciliation to our loan file fails: paper shows £118.698m PWLB at both dates; our file shows zero at 31.3.25 and £61.6m at 01.01.26 — all loans in our file have Start dates on or after 1 April 2025. Loan-book claim is out of the email.

Financing-cost ratio and balance-sheet identity are internal only.

officer.subject: The £5m off your LOBO row — twelve refused calls we've logged since spring
officer.body:
Hi Richard,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, and every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are some thoughts on the 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy you took to Cabinet on 11 March. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your strategy is well laid out and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The line that jumped out is halfway down Table 3.1 in your appendix: LOBOs at £5m on 31 March 2025 and zero on 1 January 2026. Whether that was a call by the lender or a discharge from your side isn't something the paper says — it's your file, not ours, so this isn't a question. What we can offer is what's happened elsewhere in the same window. Twelve LOBO calls have gone into councils we've read since the spring, at ten authorities including Kent, Tameside, Newcastle, York, Bath and North East Somerset, Bridgend, Newport, Harrow, Staffordshire and Wolverhampton, and every one of the twelve has been repaid at par rather than accepted at the revised rate. If it's useful to see which lenders have moved and when, the tracker is at pwlbtoday.org/lobo-tracker.

The rest of that same 3.1 table sets the shape at 1 January: £109.5m from other local authorities, £118.7m from PWLB, no LOBO. So of £228.2m of external borrowing, 48% is now LA-to-LA and typically very short-dated. The monthly PWLB data at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity is the other half of that market — every loan drawn by every council, with rates — which lets you see whether the LA book is thinning or thickening before you go to roll, not after. Thin months (May in particular this year) were only visible across the whole sector.

Your section 3.3 carries the MUFG view dated 22 December 2025, with 5-year PWLB at 4.60% in March 2026 tapering to 4.10% by late 2027 on a Bank Rate path of 3.75% down to 3.25%. The dashboard at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard shows the certainty rate at each fixing today, so it takes about ten seconds to see how much of that path has already priced in. That direction of travel matters more when the book is short-dated than when it's long.

None of it needs a meeting or a subscription. On training, three look most relevant given the shape of the strategy: LOBO loans, given the row that has just come off; Interest rate risk, for the short-dated LA book; and our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
